USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the existing Section 301 tariffs in place and stay at the table. Do not raise List 3 from 10% to 25% while a possible Trump–Xi summit is still being lined up, and do not roll back duties or trade the Huawei/Meng cases for a purchase-heavy memorandum. Push the next Beijing/Washington round for written, enforceable commitments on IP, forced tech transfer, subsidies, and a tariff snapback before any Mar-a-Lago signing.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly negative for the United States because the current state of the dispute is more leverage than existential risk. The U.S. already has 25% duties on ~$50B and 10% on ~$200B of Chinese goods (timeline 2018-07-06, 2018-08-23, 2018-09-24) and twice delayed the List 3 hike from a position of strength after the G20 truce and again on 2019-02-24. China’s growth is the weakest in decades (2018 GDP 6.6%, Q4 6.4%), industrial profits turned negative in November 2018, and provincial targets were cut — so Beijing has a stronger incentive to deal than Washington does. U.S. macro is not in a trade-war recession: Michigan sentiment recovered to 98.4 in March, VIX is 13.41, and CPI is contained, even as industrial production slipped ~1% and 10-year yields fell to 2.61%. The offsetting U.S. costs are real but sectoral: China’s matching retaliation hit soy, autos, and aircraft (2018-04-04, 2018-07-06, 2018-09-24); China typically takes ~60% of U.S. soy exports and bought almost none for months, cash prices fell below cost, and 2019 crop-insurance prices dropped to $9.54. That is political pain, not a systemic threat — hence about −0.25, not −0.5. Action should stay near zero because talks are the live instrument: Trump reported progress on IP, tech transfer, agriculture, services, and currency and delayed the March 1 hike pending more work and a possible Mar-a-Lago summit; Reuters/NYT reporting through late February still shows no signed text and no agreed enforcement, with China offering purchases (soy, LNG, chips) more readily than structural change. Hiking now would likely kill a still-open negotiation and invite broader retaliation that hits the farm belt again; conceding purchases or rolling back tariffs before written snapback language would repeat the May 2018 “on hold” collapse (2018-05-19 / 2018-05-29). Huawei/Meng is a separate legal track (DOJ charges 2019-01-28; Canada opened extradition 2019-03-01) that should not be bargained away for a cosmetic deal. Negotiate, hold the tariff stock, and condition any summit on enforceable text.
key_factors: Existing $250B Section 301 coverage still in force after two delays of the List 3 10%→25% hike
China under clearer growth stress (2018 GDP 6.6%, Q4 6.4%, industrial profits negative) than the U.S. (sentiment 98.4, VIX 13.4)
Farm-belt retaliation is the main U.S. vulnerability (soy collapse, $9.6B aid) but is also the purchase lever in talks
Structural IP/tech-transfer/subsidy issues and an enforcement/snapback mechanism remain unsigned
Huawei/Meng extradition and Canadian detainee track is a live second front that should stay off the tariff table

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25% (previously tied to the March 1 end of the 90-day window).
Another round of talks (through Feb 15). Progress reported on purchases; enforcement mechanism still disputed.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment recovered to 98.4 in March 2019 after the January dip to 91.2.
VIX closed 13.41 on 2019-03-13, back to pre-escalation calm after the Dec 2018 spike.
U.S. goods imports from China fell from $52.1B (Oct 2018) to $31.1B (Mar 2019), about -40% over the window.
10-year Treasury yield 2.61% on 2019-03-13, down ~38bp over the lookback; curve flattened versus 2.45% 2-year.

Despite progress touted by Trump, the Chinese have still yet to make written commitments to core issues; no official agreement signed; enforcement mechanism not agreed; China ready to commit to billions in soy, beef, LNG purchases while resisting more structural change.
China 2018 GDP growth 6.6% (lowest since 1990); Q4 2018 growth 6.4%, lowest quarterly reading since the 2008 crisis; December exports contracted as tariffs began to bite.
China typically bought ~60% of U.S. soy exports (~$12B); first 10 months of 2018 shipments to China fell ~62%; $9.6B market-facilitation aid only partly offsets farm losses.
Canada proceeded with Meng extradition hearing in early March 2019 even as a trade deal was discussed; Huawei criminal cases continue independently of tariff talks.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep negotiating continuously with Lighthizer/Mnuchin and do not open a new tariff or hostage-style front while the List 3 hike is still suspended. Use additional agricultural and energy purchases as bargaining chips only against a written path to freeze or roll back U.S. Section 301 rates, and keep structural/IP language narrow enough that it does not lock in U.S. snapback rights or gut industrial-policy space. Hold the Meng/Huawei file on a separate legal-diplomatic track rather than trading it into an unfinished commercial deal.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. Combined U.S. Section 301 coverage is already ~$250B (List 1/2 at 25%, List 3 at 10% from 24 Sep 2018), and U.S. customs imports from China fell from $52.1B in Oct 2018 to $31.1B in Mar 2019 (−40%). Official factory PMI dropped to 49.2 in Feb with new export orders at 45.2, the weakest since 2009; Feb exports plunged 20.7% y/y (Jan–Feb still ~−5% after holiday smoothing), and 2018 GDP slowed to 6.6% with a 6.0–6.5% 2019 target. Huawei is under firm-level legal and 5G pressure (DOJ charges 28 Jan; Canada authorized Meng extradition proceedings 1 Mar). That cluster sits just below the +0.5 CHN anchor because there is no FX-reserve crisis in the available data, the Jan 1 / Mar 1 List 3 hike to 25% was delayed (24 Feb / 1 Mar), and talks are described as being in their “final weeks.” Escalation now would likely invite the postponed 25% hike and further export-hub job losses already visible in PMI employment. Maximal concession is also premature: Lighthizer told the Senate Finance Committee on 12 Mar that “major issues” (enforcement, IP/tech transfer, SOE subsidies, currency) remain open, China is pushing for full tariff removal, and the U.S. has not locked a matching rollback. Purchase talk has already featured in every 2019 round; converting that into a one-sided concede_purchases label without a reciprocal tariff path would spend leverage before the text is done. Negotiate — no new commitments beyond exploring a purchase-for-tariff-freeze package — is therefore the stance that matches a +0.42 threat reading.
key_factors: ~$250B of Chinese goods still under Section 301; List 3 10%→25% hike delayed but not cancelled
Sharp contraction in the U.S. China-import channel and Feb 2019 export/PMI slump
Huawei/Meng legal and 5G campaign is a separate firm-level and tech-sovereignty threat
Talks are live and in 'final weeks' but enforcement and structural issues remain unresolved
Unilateral escalation or one-sided purchase/structural giveaways would worsen, not hedge, the growth and legitimacy risk

sources_cited.excerpt: List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
G20 Buenos Aires dinner: 90-day negotiation window; planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended. Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
Trump tweets that talks have made substantial progress and further delays the scheduled List 3 hike from 10% to 25%.
Lighthizer and Mnuchin in Beijing for high-level talks. Purchase commitments discussed; enforcement and structural IP/tech-transfer issues unresolved.
U.S. imports of goods from China fell from 52081 (2018-10) to 31079 (2019-03), a ~40% decline over the window.
February exports fell 20.7 percent from a year earlier, the largest decline since February 2016; government targeting 6.0 to 6.5 percent growth in 2019 after 6.6 percent in 2018.

Lighthizer said major issues remain unresolved, hoped talks were in the 'final weeks,' and that China was pushing hard for all American tariffs to be removed while enforcement was still the biggest obstacle.
Meng extradition hearing opens in Vancouver during trade talks; Beijing sees the arrest as political and Huawei as a national champion under U.S. pressure.
